body:
**24 November 2026 · 231.08 · Limit unsent data on an established Linux TCP socket**

Local/host-only Linux 6.18.57 x86_64, private IPv4 loopback. Changed only the accepted Reno bulk socket's TCP_NOTSENT_LOWAT from inherited (system value 4,294,967,295 B) to 16,384 B. The send and receive buffers stayed at 3,939,840 and 32,768 B in the stalled-reader fixture. Each workload used 16 randomized, counterbalanced pairs, eight in each order. All first attempts retained.

With a 1 MiB bulk offer and the reader paused, immediately readable data stayed at 24,576 B in all 32 attempts. Unsent bytes fell from 1,024,000 to 16,384. When the application sent a priority marker before the remaining bulk, the receiver saw 1,048,576 → 40,960 B ahead of the marker in every pair. Both arms subsequently delivered the exact full payload, marker and EOF. This establishes the amount of already-queued work a same-stream reply must wait behind.

A separate, short 4 MiB transfer ran alongside 16 fresh loopback connections per attempt. Receiver-verified throughput medians were 514 → 569 MiB/s. Median within-pair change +15.5% (95% whole-pair bootstrap +0.8% to +26.9%, 12/16 wins, 10,000 resamples, seed 77). All 256 fresh requests per arm completed. Pooled fresh p95/p99 were 0.390/1.836 → 0.560/0.877 ms. 249/256 control and 256/256 candidate requests completed before bulk EOF. Fresh requests were closed-loop; elapsed times include client scheduling. Packet drops, CPU/GiB and runnable time were unmeasured. Millisecond-scale transfers on this host cannot predict a VM or peer gain.

Verdict: the per-socket limit bounds how much bulk can queue ahead of a later reply without shrinking SO_SNDBUF. Fresh p95 rose on independent connections in this short fixture. Keep stock for the four-vCPU baseline. Before considering a guest-side cap, capture unsent bytes on the actual bulk sender and verify whether fresh traffic shares that socket.
